query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a multi-constituent silicide-based coating on refractory high-entropy alloys will significantly improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a stable and dense protective scale, reducing oxygen ingress and embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or solution-treated Mo-Nb-Ta-W-based refractory high-entropy alloy with standard surface finishing.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, stable, multi-constituent silicide-based coating via fused slurry or pack cementation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at approximately 1200 °C for up to 150 hours under continuous or cyclic heating conditions relevant to high-temperature structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense silicide scale that limits oxygen diffusion into the underlying alloy.
generation.mechanism: Upon high-temperature exposure, the silicide coating forms a protective surface layer that suppresses oxidation kinetics and prevents oxygen-induced embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the uncoated alloy, coated samples exhibit at least an order of magnitude decrease in mass gain under identical test conditions, along with improved retention of mechanical integrity (reduced cracking and minimized embrittlement).
generation.baseline: An uncoated control of the same refractory high-entropy alloy composition and heat treatment history, evaluated under the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to persist under service up to ~1200 °C for moderate durations (~150 hours); long-term exposure or higher temperatures may require additional validation.
generation.uncertainty: Variations in substrate chemistry, longer exposure times, or more severe thermal cycling could alter scale integrity and require further studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical RHEA specimens, one set coated with the silicide-based layer and one set uncoated. Expose both sets to air at 1200 °C for 150 hours, including repeated thermal cycles (e.g., 10 cycles). Characterize mass change and mechanical properties (hardness/strength) before and after testing.
measurements: Mass gain measurements to determine oxidation kinetics
Cross-sectional microscopy and elemental analysis to evaluate oxide layer thickness and composition
High-temperature mechanical testing (compression or microhardness) to assess property retention
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain and superior mechanical retention compared with the uncoated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [,,,,,,]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [,,,,,,]. For example, Mo25Nb25Ta25W25 and Mo20Nb20Ta20W20V20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs []. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [,]. decision.trend: Early work (PMC6513993) demonstrated that forming stable CrTaO4-based oxide scales can improve long-term oxidation resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys. Later studies (PMC7475834) explored fused slurry silicide coatings to mitigate oxidation in RHEAs. Research on high-entropy borides (PMC9101925) and high-Cr RHEA compositions (PMC10142552) further highlighted the benefits of tailored protective layers. Despite these efforts, consistently achieving robust, crack-free barriers that provide oxidation resistance in severe cyclic environments and extremely high temperatures remains challenging.
decision.unsolved: Ensuring continuous, defect-free, and protective oxide or silicide layers that remain stable over protracted service times at ultra-high temperatures, without compromising mechanical integrity, has not been conclusively achieved. Controlling scale adhesion, thickness, and longevity remains a key challenge.
decision.lever: Deposit a thin, stable, multi-constituent silicide-based coating (via fused slurry or pack cementation) designed to form a dense, slow-growing silicide scale in air above 1200°C for up to 150 hours; evaluate spallation resistance and oxygen ingress via cross-sectional microscopy and mass-gain measurements.
decision.why: Silicide coatings have shown efficacy in retarding oxidation (PMC7475834), forming continuous protective layers that limit oxygen diffusion even at high temperatures. This approach directly addresses the challenge of oxygen embrittlement and leverages prior successes in fused slurry coating techniques for refractory HEAs, providing a clear route to enhance surface stability without extensive bulk alloy modifications.
